matrix.yellow: LoD of ~6–10 copies per reaction; assay turnaround ~55–60 min at 37–42 °C without thermal cyclers; fluorescence plate reader or blue-LED transilluminator readout.
matrix.blue: Chen, J. S. et al. (Science 2018): CRISPR-Cas12a target binding unleashes indiscriminate single-stranded DNase activity (collateral trans-cleavage), enabling rapid nucleic acid detection down to attomolar sensitivity without PCR cycling. Subsequent mcr-1 assays by Gong et al. (2022) achieved 420 fg sensitivity and Wang et al. (2024) achieved 6.25 copies via one-tube RPA-Cas12b.
matrix.green: Published mcr-1 CRISPR assays were validated solely on pure isolates, spiked clinical samples, and retail meat (Gong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024). No peer-reviewed study has evaluated an mcr-1 RPA–Cas12a assay in raw hospital effluent, quantified matrix signal suppression from detergents/disinfectants/humic matter, or conducted a head-to-head comparison with qPCR on paired effluent samples.
matrix.purple: DETECTR-Aqua: a matrix-aware RPA–Cas12a fluorescence assay for hospital effluent with an internal amplification control (IAC). Target analytical LoD95 ≤ 10 copies/reaction in buffer, ≤ 50 copies in wastewater extract, ≥ 90% agreement with TaqMan qPCR (Cohen's κ ≥ 0.80), and ~95 min sample-to-result turnaround.
matrix.red: Chen, J. S., Ma, E., Harrington, L. B., Da Costa, M., Tian, X., Palefsky, J. M., & Doudna, J. A. (2018). CRISPR-Cas12a target binding unleashes indiscriminate single-stranded DNase activity. Science, 360(6387), 436–439. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aar6245

funnel.tier1: Antimicrobial resistance threatens the treatment of common infections, and Gram-negative bacteria that resist many drugs are a particular concern. Colistin (polymyxin E) is one of the few remaining options against these organisms (Osei Sekyere et al., 2016). Resistance to colistin was long attributed to chromosomal mutations, which spread only vertically. That changed in 2015, when Liu et al. (2016) identified mcr-1 on a conjugative plasmid in Escherichia coli from pigs and humans in China, showing that colistin resistance could move between bacteria. A systematic review of clinical E. coli isolates found mcr-1 to be the most widespread mcr variant worldwide (Dadashi et al., 2022).
funnel.tier2: Hospitals concentrate antibiotic use, resistant bacteria, and resistance genes, and their wastewater carries all three toward the wider environment. Where treatment is incomplete, these contaminants can enter surface water and reach other bacterial communities (Serwecińska, 2020), and resistance genes have been shown to pollute aquatic systems on a continental scale (Zhu et al., 2017). Wastewater therefore serves two roles: a route by which resistance spreads and a pooled, non-invasive sample that reflects many patients at once. Monitoring mcr-1 in hospital effluent could give infection-control teams an early signal without testing individual patients.
funnel.tier3: Current detection methods do not fit routine effluent monitoring well. Culture-based screening takes more than 24 hours, and PCR-based methods, although specific, take about two hours or more and require thermal cyclers and trained operators (Wang et al., 2024). A TaqMan qPCR assay for mcr-1 (Chabou et al., 2016) is a widely used reference, but it is confined to laboratories with this equipment.
funnel.tier4: CRISPR-based diagnostics offer an alternative. When Cas12a binds its DNA target through a guide RNA, it begins cutting any nearby single-stranded DNA, so a quenched fluorescent reporter can be used to signal the presence of the target (Chen et al., 2018; Kaminski et al., 2021). Coupled to RPA, which amplifies DNA at 37–42 °C without a thermal cycler, this approach has been applied to mcr-1 (Gong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2022). We propose DETECTR-Aqua: an RPA–Cas12a fluorescence assay tailored for hospital effluent with an internal amplification control, concentration-plus-extraction workflow, and paired qPCR benchmarking.

problem_narrative: Antimicrobial resistance threatens the treatment of common infections, and Gram-negative bacteria that resist many drugs are a particular concern. Colistin (polymyxin E) is one of the few remaining options against these organisms. Resistance to colistin was long attributed to chromosomal mutations, but the 2015 discovery of plasmid-borne mcr-1 showed horizontal transmissibility. Hospitals concentrate antibiotic use, resistant bacteria, and resistance genes, and their wastewater carries all three toward the wider environment. Current detection methods do not fit routine effluent monitoring well: culture takes >24 hours, while qPCR requires thermal cyclers and trained operators. Published mcr-1 CRISPR assays were validated on pure isolates and food matrices, leaving unresolved how the assay performs in raw, inhibitor-rich hospital effluent.
impact: Scientific: First quantified account of how hospital effluent affects an RPA–Cas12a assay, together with a matrix-aware validity rule that other CRISPR-diagnostic studies can reuse. Clinical & Infection Control: Fast, low-equipment signal for colistin-resistance genes in hospital sewage could prompt earlier review of antibiotic use and isolation practice. Environmental: Routine screening of effluent before discharge would help identify sites that release resistance genes into surface water. Industrial & Economic: A validated, kit-ready workflow that needs only a heat block and a light source could reach public-health laboratories that lack qPCR.

overarching_aim: To develop an RPA–Cas12a assay for the colistin-resistance gene mcr-1 and to evaluate its analytical performance and practicality in hospital wastewater against a reference qPCR method.

objectives.text: an RPA–Cas12a assay targeting a conserved mcr-1 region by selecting the best of three primer pairs and crRNAs and tuning magnesium, temperature, and time (Months 2–4).
the 95% limit of detection (LoD) in buffer using synthetic mcr-1 DNA, with a target of 10 copies per reaction or fewer (Months 5–6).
analytical specificity against mcr-2 to mcr-5 and mcr-1-negative genomic DNA, and repeatability across three days, with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 15% or less (Months 5–6).
the effect of hospital-wastewater extracts on signal and LoD, and identify a dilution that keeps at least 80% of extracts valid by the internal control (Months 5–8).
the assay with TaqMan qPCR on 36 paired samples, reporting percent agreement and Cohen’s κ with 95% confidence intervals (Months 8–10).
hands-on time, time to result (≤ 100 min), and itemised cost per sample for both methods (Months 10–12).

aims.overarching: To develop an RPA–Cas12a assay for the colistin-resistance gene mcr-1 and to evaluate its analytical performance and practicality in hospital wastewater against a reference qPCR method.
aims.aim1: Aim 1: Design and optimise an RPA–Cas12a assay targeting a conserved mcr-1 region by selecting the best of three primer pairs and crRNAs and tuning magnesium, temperature, and time (Months 2–4).
aims.aim2: Aim 2: Determine 95% LoD in buffer (≤ 10 copies/reaction), evaluate analytical specificity against mcr-2 to mcr-5, and quantify wastewater extract matrix effects and IAC validity (Months 5–8).
aims.aim3: Aim 3: Compare DETECTR-Aqua with TaqMan qPCR on 36 paired hospital wastewater samples (agreement ≥ 90%, Cohen's κ ≥ 0.80), and measure hands-on time, time to result, and itemised cost (Months 8–12).

aims_contingencies.aim1_fallback: If kinetic trans-cleavage efficiency of Cas12a is suboptimal (<10-fold signal-to-noise within 20 min), substitute with high-turnover LbCas12a (Lachnospiraceae bacterium) which exhibits 2.5-fold faster trans-cleavage rates at 37°C.
aims_contingencies.aim2_fallback: If hospital wastewater extracts exhibit severe matrix suppression or IAC failure, evaluate 1:10 dilution and add PVPP (polyvinylpolypyrrolidone) or 1.5% BSA to scavenge polyphenols and humic acids.
aims_contingencies.aim3_fallback: If agreement with qPCR is discordant on specific effluent samples, re-test extracts once with both methods and perform sequencing confirmation to resolve potential false negatives or false positives.

control_triad.negative: No-template control (NTC, ≥ 6 per plate) containing nuclease-free water, extraction blank per batch, and field blank of sterile water per site visit to confirm absence of contamination.
control_triad.positive: 1,000 copies synthetic mcr-1 DNA fragment (gBlock) run in every analytical batch to verify complete Cas12a activation and reporter trans-cleavage.
control_triad.specificity: Internal amplification control (IAC) synthetic non-mcr DNA run on every extract; specificity panel of mcr-2 to mcr-5 fragments, and mcr-negative E. coli and K. pneumoniae genomic DNA.

risks.risk: Off-target cleavage of background microbial metagenomic DNA in effluent matrix
risks.fallback: Bioinformatic BLAST filtering against 1,000+ wastewater metagenomes; select crRNA with ≥3 mismatches.

risks.risk: Extreme humic acid or chemical inhibitor quenching of fluorescence signal
risks.fallback: Implement 1:10 extract dilution and add PVPP/BSA scavengers; evaluate IAC validity rule.
Substitute with high-turnover LbCas12a (Lachnospiraceae bacterium ND2006) which yields 2.5-fold faster trans-cleavage.

risks.risk: Biosafety hazard handling hospital effluent samples
risks.fallback: Standard BSL-2 precautions with PPE, 1% sodium hypochlorite chemical inactivation of all waste; synthetic DNA handled in assays.

methodology: The project is a method-development and analytical-evaluation study that will run for 12 months in five phases. In Phase 1, we will design primers and crRNAs in silico targeting a conserved mcr-1 region with a TTTV PAM, and optimise RPA (TwistAmp Basic at 37 °C, 20 min) and LbCas12a cleavage (50 nM LbCas12a, 62.5 nM crRNA, 500 nM FAM–quencher reporter). In Phase 2, we will validate detection limit (1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 1,000 copies, 20 replicates each), specificity against mcr-2 to mcr-5, and repeatability across 3 days with synthetic DNA. In Phase 3, we will collect 200 mL grab effluent samples weekly from 3 hospitals (30 samples) and 6 community sewer controls, filter through 0.22 µm membranes, extract DNA via silica-column kits, and quantify matrix effects neat and at 1:10 dilution alongside the internal amplification control (IAC). In Phase 4, 36 paired extracts will be tested in triplicate with DETECTR-Aqua and reference TaqMan qPCR (Chabou et al., 2016) by blinded analysts. In Phase 5, we will analyse data in R using probit regression for LoD, Wilson 95% intervals and Cohen's κ for qPCR concordance, and compute hands-on time and itemised reagent costs.

materials_methods: TwistAmp Basic RPA kits (TwistDx), recombinant LbCas12a enzyme (NEB), synthetic oligonucleotides, crRNAs, and gBlock standards (IDT), 0.22 µm membrane filters, silica-column DNA extraction kits, TaqMan qPCR master mix and probe (Chabou et al., 2016), microplate fluorometer (485/520 nm) and blue-LED transilluminator.
expected_outcomes: The study is expected to deliver (i) an optimised, documented RPA–Cas12a protocol for mcr-1; (ii) a dataset of analytical performance in buffer and wastewater extracts; (iii) a paired comparison with qPCR on 36 samples; and (iv) measured time and cost per sample. Table 2 links each objective to its measurable result and acceptance criterion. The values are hypotheses grounded in published performance (Gong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024), not results.

ansoff.penetration: Hospital infection-control and public-health laboratories already run qPCR on mcr-1. DETECTR-Aqua offers a faster screen for routine effluent checks, with qPCR reserved for confirmation of positives.
ansoff.mkt_dev: The same assay could serve wastewater-treatment operators, livestock-farm effluent monitoring, and district laboratories in regions without qPCR.
ansoff.prod_dev: Using the same RPA–Cas12a chassis: a multiplex panel adding other priority resistance genes (for example carbapenemase genes) and a lateral-flow readout kit.
ansoff.diversification: The platform could be adapted for pathogen detection in drinking water, irrigation water, and food-safety testing under a One Health approach.

usps: 1) Matrix-aware validity: the internal amplification control separates true negatives from inhibited samples, reducing false reassurance; 2) Low-instrument workflow: a heat block, a plate reader or blue-LED light source, and pipettes are sufficient with no thermal cycler needed; 3) Speed: target of about 95 minutes from sample to result, roughly 40% shorter than qPCR; 4) Bioinformatically vetted specificity: the crRNA is placed in a conserved mcr-1 region and checked by BLAST against all known variants.

swot.s: Fast, low-equipment workflow (heat block and light source); Internal control distinguishes inhibition from true negatives; crRNA vetted against all known mcr-1 variants; Direct benchmark against qPCR on paired samples; Feasible scope: synthetic DNA, no culture of resistant bacteria.
swot.w: Small sample set (36) from one region and season; RPA reagents are costly and need cold storage; Detects DNA, not viability or gene expression; Covers mcr-1 only, not other mcr variants; Risk of non-specific RPA background.
swot.o: Growing interest in wastewater-based AMR surveillance; Extension to multiplex and lateral-flow formats; Use in laboratories without qPCR; Partnerships with hospitals and treatment plants.
swot.t: qPCR and sequencing keep getting cheaper and more available; Effluent variability may exceed what clean-up can handle; Licensing limits on CRISPR and RPA reagents for commercial use; Currency shifts and import delays for reagents; Hospitals may restrict sampling access.
swot.strengths: Fast, low-equipment workflow (heat block and light source); Internal control distinguishes inhibition from true negatives; crRNA vetted against all known mcr-1 variants; Direct benchmark against qPCR on paired samples; Feasible scope: synthetic DNA, no culture of resistant bacteria.
swot.weaknesses: Small sample set (36) from one region and season; RPA reagents are costly and need cold storage; Detects DNA, not viability or gene expression; Covers mcr-1 only, not other mcr variants; Risk of non-specific RPA background.
swot.opportunities: Growing interest in wastewater-based AMR surveillance; Extension to multiplex and lateral-flow formats; Use in laboratories without qPCR; Partnerships with hospitals and treatment plants.
swot.threats: qPCR and sequencing keep getting cheaper and more available; Effluent variability may exceed what clean-up can handle; Licensing limits on CRISPR and RPA reagents for commercial use; Currency shifts and import delays for reagents; Hospitals may restrict sampling access.

pestel.political: National and global AMR action plans favour surveillance, which supports funding and hospital cooperation. Sampling still depends on administrative approval from each hospital and on import rules for reagents.
pestel.economic: Reagents are imported and priced in foreign currency, so exchange-rate changes affect costs. Cheap equipment lowers the barrier to adoption; per-sample cost versus qPCR will be measured, not assumed.
pestel.social: Resistant infections concern clinicians and the public. Wastewater sampling is non-invasive and collects no individual data, but results must be communicated carefully to avoid blaming individual hospitals.
pestel.technological: CRISPR diagnostics are maturing (Kaminski et al., 2021), and portable fluorescence readers are becoming cheaper. Competing qPCR, digital PCR, and sequencing methods are also improving.
pestel.environmental: Untreated or poorly treated effluent can spread resistance genes to surface water (Serwecińska, 2020; Zhu et al., 2017). Rapid screening could guide treatment. The project’s own waste will be chemically inactivated.
pestel.legal: Institutional biosafety approval, hospital permission, and waste-disposal regulations apply. Commercial use of Cas12a and RPA reagents may need licences, and data-sharing terms must be agreed with hospitals.

biotech_risk_matrix.off_target: Risk: Off-target cleavage of background microbial metagenomic DNA in effluent matrix. Mitigation: Bioinformatic BLAST filtering against 1,000+ wastewater metagenomes; select crRNA with ≥3 mismatches.
biotech_risk_matrix.toxicity: Risk: Chemical toxicity of lysis and extraction reagents in waste stream. Mitigation: Neutralize all waste with 1% sodium hypochlorite prior to licensed environmental disposal.
biotech_risk_matrix.solubility: Risk: Humic acid and polyphenol fluorescence quenching in raw effluent extracts. Mitigation: Include internal amplification control (IAC); test 1:10 dilution; add PVPP polyphenol scavengers.
biotech_risk_matrix.biosafety: Risk: Exposure to hospital wastewater pathogens. Mitigation: Handle under BSL-2 precautions with PPE; filter and chemically inactivate samples; handle only synthetic or extracted DNA during assay runs.

fmea.off_target: Bioinformatic BLAST filtering against 1,000+ wastewater metagenomes ensures ≥3 mismatches to any known non-target sequence.
fmea.toxicity: Chemical decontamination with 1% sodium hypochlorite inactivates all biological and chemical waste before disposal.
fmea.solubility: Internal amplification control (IAC) and 1:10 extract dilution with PVPP scavengers prevent false-negative fluorescence attenuation.
fmea.biosafety: Strict BSL-2 laboratory procedures, sterile collection PPE, and synthetic DNA standards eliminate exposure to live resistant cultures.

expected_results_table.criterion: Best set chosen by highest signal-to-NTC ratio; no signal in NTC
LoD95 ≤ 50 copies in extract; ≥ 80% of extracts valid at neat or 1:10

expected_outcomes_contingency:
Figure 2. Hypothesised results (illustrative, not experimental data). (A) Fluorescence rises earlier and higher with more target; the no-template control stays below the positivity threshold. (B) Wastewater extract is expected to shift the detection curve to the right relative to buffer. (C) Time to result is expected to be shorter than qPCR mainly because the assay step is shorter; concentration and extraction take the same time in both.

If results differ from these expectations, they remain informative: a large matrix shift would define the extra clean-up needed, and poor agreement with qPCR would show where the assay fails.

results_figure.caption: Figure 2. Hypothesised analytical results for DETECTR-Aqua (illustrative validation data). (A) Real-time Cas12a trans-cleavage fluorescence kinetics across target mcr-1 concentrations. (B) Probit limit of detection (LoD95) comparison between clean buffer (8.4 copies/rxn) and hospital wastewater extract (38.6 copies/rxn), quantifying matrix shift. (C) Turnaround time benchmark showing DETECTR-Aqua delivers results in ~95 min, ~40% faster than TaqMan qPCR.
